notes.title: DC Circuit Fundamentals — complete revision notes

sections.heading: Charge, current, voltage, power
bullets: I = dQ/dt; conventional current flows + to −; electrons drift the other way.
V = work per unit charge (volt = J/C); voltage is always a difference between two points.
P = VI = I²R = V²/R; energy = P·t — the unit ladder W·h → kW·h is how bills are computed.

sections.heading: Resistors & networks
bullets: Series: R_eq = ΣR (same current); parallel: 1/R_eq = Σ1/R (same voltage).
Two parallel shortcut: R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂).
Voltage divider: V_out = V_in·R₂/(R₁+R₂); current divider: I₁ = I·R₂/(R₁+R₂).
Conductance G = 1/R; siemens S.

sections.heading: Kirchhoff's laws (BEEE Module 2 preview)
bullets: KCL at a node: ΣI_in = ΣI_out — charge cannot pile up.
KVL around a loop: ΣV = 0 — energy around a closed path is zero.
Sign discipline: assign directions first, let algebra confirm (negative result = opposite direction).

sections.heading: Practical DC
bullets: Real sources: V_terminal = V_emf − I·r_internal — terminal drops under load.
Wheatstone bridge balance: R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄ ⇒ null detector current = 0.
Maximum power transfer: R_load = R_internal, efficiency then = 50%.

questions.prompt: Find R_eq of 6 Ω ∥ (4 Ω + 8 Ω) in series with 3 Ω.
A 12 V source with internal resistance 1 Ω feeds a 5 Ω load. Load voltage?
Voltage divider: 10 V across 10 kΩ + 4 kΩ; output across 4 kΩ?
Two 100 Ω lamps in parallel on 50 V. Total power?
solution: Check: R_eq = 50 Ω, P = V²/R = 2500/50 = 50 W ✓

sections.heading: Superposition
bullets: Response in a linear network with several sources = sum of responses from each source alone.
Kill other sources: voltage sources → short, current sources → open.
Never turn OFF the source you're analysing across; power is NOT superposable (recompute VI at the end).

sections.heading: Thevenin & Norton
bullets: Thevenin: any two-terminal linear network ⇒ V_TH (open-circuit voltage) + R_TH (dead sources, look-in resistance).
Norton: I_N = V_TH/R_TH in parallel with same R_TH — source transformation between the two.
Steps: remove load → find V_OC → kill sources → find R_TH → reattach load: I_L = V_TH/(R_TH+R_L).

sections.heading: Maximum power & reciprocity
bullets: Max power in R_L when R_L = R_TH; P_max = V_TH²/(4R_TH).
Efficiency at max power = 50% — you cannot win both.
Reciprocity (unilateral networks): transfer ratio same when source and detector swap.

sections.heading: Millman & compensation
bullets: Millman: common voltage V = Σ(Vᵢ/Rᵢ) / Σ(1/Rᵢ) for parallel branches.
Tellegen's theorem: Σ v_k i_k = 0 over all branches (power conservation, any topology).

questions.prompt: Find Thevenin voltage across the open terminals of a 10 V source in series with 2 kΩ (terminals after the resistor).
solution: Open terminals ⇒ no current ⇒ no drop across 2 kΩ.
Kill source (short) ⇒ look-in sees 2 kΩ ⇒ R_TH = 2 kΩ.

questions.prompt: Network seen from load has V_TH = 12 V, R_TH = 3 Ω. Load R_L = 6 Ω — current and load power?
Two batteries 10 V/1 Ω and 6 V/1 Ω drive a 7 Ω load in the SAME aiding direction. Superpose current.
solution: Only the 10 V source active (6 V shorted): I′ = 10/(1+1+7) = 10/9 A.
Only the 6 V source active (10 V shorted): I″ = 6/(1+1+7) = 6/9 A.
Aiding direction: I = I′ + I″ = 16/9 ≈ 1.78 A — same as direct (10+6)/9 ✓

questions.prompt: For max power, R_L must equal…? State P_max when V_TH = 20 V, R_TH = 10 Ω.

sections.heading: p-n diode behaviour
bullets: Forward bias (p to +): barrier shrinks, diffusion current grows exponentially.
Reverse bias: only tiny reverse saturation current Iₛ flows (until breakdown).
Shockley equation I = Iₛ(e^{V/ηV_T} − 1); V_T ≈ 26 mV at 300 K, η ≈ 1 (Si).
Piecewise model: 0.7 V constant-drop for Si, 0.3 V for Ge — exam default.

sections.heading: Rectifiers
bullets: Half-wave: output frequency = f_in, peak inverse voltage = V_m.
Full-wave centre-tap: PIV = 2V_m; bridge: PIV = V_m, no centre tap needed.
Average DC (full-wave) = 2V_m/π ≈ 0.636 V_m; half-wave = V_m/π.
Ripple factor improves with C filter: f_ripple = 2f for full-wave (100 Hz on 50 Hz mains).

sections.heading: Special diodes
bullets: Zener: operated in reverse breakdown, regulates V across R_L — series R limits current.
LED: forward-biased, ~1.8–3 V depending on colour; needs series resistor.
Photodiode: reverse-biased, photocurrent ∝ light; solar cell delivers power.

questions.prompt: A Si diode in series with 1 kΩ across 10 V (ideal-ish with 0.7 V drop). Current?
Full-wave rectifier, V_m = 15 V. Average output voltage (no filter)?
PIV required for bridge rectifier with secondary V_m = 20 V?
solution: In a bridge, two diodes conduct while two block.
PIV = V_m = 20 V (centre-tap design would need 40 V).

questions.prompt: Zener at 5.1 V regulates a 12 V supply through 340 Ω with R_L = 1 kΩ. Estimate load current.
solution: (Series current = (12−5.1)/340 ≈ 20 mA ⇒ I_Z ≈ 15 mA — Zener well in regulation.)

sections.heading: Regions & symbols
bullets: BJT = NPN or PNP; terminals E, B, C; current gain β = I_C/I_B (≈100 typical), α = I_C/I_E.
I_E = I_B + I_C always.
Regions: cutoff (both junctions reverse) — switch OFF; active (EB fwd, CB reverse) — amplifier; saturation (both fwd) — switch ON.

sections.heading: Biasing for stable Q-point
bullets: Fixed bias is thermally unstable; voltage-divider bias with stiff divider (βR_E ≫ R₂) makes I_C ≈ V_TH/R_E almost β-independent.
Load line: I_C = (V_CC − V_CE)/R_C; Q-point sits mid-line for max swing.
Emitter resistor gives negative feedback: I_C↑ ⇒ V_E↑ ⇒ V_BE↓ ⇒ I_C↓.

sections.heading: Small-signal view
bullets: r_π = β·V_T/I_C (≈ 2.6 kΩ at 1 mA, β=100); g_m = I_C/V_T.
CE amplifier: A_v ≈ −g_m·(R_C ∥ R_L) — inverting gain.
Common collector (emitter follower): gain ≈ 1, high input Z — used as buffer.

questions.prompt: β = 120, I_B = 40 µA. Find I_C and I_E.
Voltage-divider bias: V_CC = 12 V, R₁ = 47 kΩ, R₂ = 10 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ. Approx I_C.
solution: I_C ≈ I_E = 1.4 mA (almost independent of β — that's why this bias is stable).

questions.prompt: CE stage with R_C = 2.2 kΩ, I_C = 2 mA. Estimate voltage gain (β large).
In which region does a BJT act as a closed switch?
solution: V_CE(sat) ≈ 0.2 V — almost short across C–E.

sections.heading: Structure & operation
bullets: MOSFET: gate insulated by SiO₂ — voltage-controlled, essentially zero gate current.
n-channel enhancement: V_GS > V_th forms the inversion channel; drain current flows.
Cut-off: V_GS < V_th (open switch); linear/ohmic: small V_DS (resistor); saturation: pinched channel (amplifier region for depletion types — for enhancement, 'saturation' = V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_th).

sections.heading: Transfer & switching
bullets: Shockley for FET: I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)² (depletion/JFET form).
CMOS inverter: one pMOS + one nMOS — rail-to-rail output, near-zero static power.
Gate drive: C_gs charging sets switching speed; driver ICs supply the spike current.

sections.heading: Applications
bullets: MOSFET as load switch / motor driver / chopper — chosen for low R_DS(on).
Power MOSFETs in SMPS: fast, but body diode & avalanche ratings must be respected.
Comparison: BJT current-driven & higher drop; MOSFET voltage-driven & lower conduction loss at low voltage.

questions.prompt: n-channel enhancement MOSFET with V_th = 2 V: what happens at V_GS = 1 V, V_DS = 10 V?
JFET: I_DSS = 8 mA, V_P = −4 V. I_D at V_GS = −2 V?
Why does a CMOS inverter consume almost no static power?
questions.answer: One transistor is off at a time — no direct V_DD→GND path
solution: pMOS on/nMOS off for input 0; reverse for input 1.
Only dynamic power = C·V²·f during transitions.

questions.prompt: MOSFET R_DS(on) = 0.05 Ω carrying 10 A. Conduction loss?
solution: Compare BJT: V_CE(sat)≈0.2 V ⇒ 2 W? — actually 10×0.2 = 20 W — MOSFET wins at high current.

notes.title: Operational Amplifiers — complete revision notes (your biggest-gap module)

sections.heading: Ideal op-amp model (the whole game)
bullets: Two golden rules: (1) i₊ = i₋ = 0 (infinite input Z), (2) V₊ = V₋ (virtual short when negative feedback exists).
Open-loop gain A → ∞; bandwidth → ∞; output can source/sink whatever the rails allow.
Virtual short only holds WITH feedback — never apply it open-loop.

sections.heading: Core configurations
bullets: Inverting amp: A_v = −R_f/R_in; V₋ node is virtual ground.
Non-inverting: A_v = 1 + R_f/R_in; input Z huge — buffer at A_v = 1 (R_f = 0).
Summer: V_out = −R_f·(V₁/R₁ + V₂/R₂).
Integrator: C in feedback, V_out = −(1/RC)∫V_in dt; differentiator: C at input (add series R for stability).
Difference amp: V_out = (R_f/R_in)(V₂ − V₁) when resistors are matched pairs.

sections.heading: Applications & non-ideal notes
bullets: Comparator: no feedback — output saturates to rail based on which input is higher.
Schmitt trigger: positive feedback gives hysteresis — cleans noisy signals.
Non-ideal: finite GBW (gain × bandwidth constant ≈ 1 MHz class parts), slew rate limits fast edges, offset voltage shifts outputs.
Bias current path: match DC resistance seen by both inputs to cancel offset.

sections.heading: Exam problem recipe
bullets: 1) Identify feedback path. 2) Mark V₊/V₋. 3) KCL at the inverting node. 4) Solve.
If the problem gives rails (±12 V), clamp the final answer — no output exceeds the rails.
Gain bandwidth check: closed-loop gain × signal freq must sit under GBW.

questions.prompt: Inverting amplifier: R_in = 10 kΩ, R_f = 100 kΩ, V_in = 0.2 V. Find V_out.
solution: Virtual ground at V₋ = 0 ⇒ I_in = 0.2/10k = 20 µA through R_f ⇒ drop = 2 V.

questions.prompt: Non-inverting amp with R_in = 5 kΩ (to ground), R_f = 15 kΩ. Gain?
solution: No phase inversion; input impedance stays extremely high.

questions.prompt: Summing amplifier with R_f = 60 kΩ and inputs 1 kΩ (2 V), 2 kΩ (3 V)?
solution: With ±15 V rails the op-amp saturates near −15 V — always clamp.

questions.prompt: Integrator: R = 100 kΩ, C = 10 µF, constant V_in = 1 V. Rate of change of V_out?
